newsitem.title: CONGO: Brazzaville fighting eases, Gabon meeting mooted.
newsitem.headline: Brazzaville fighting eases, Gabon meeting mooted.

text.p: The battered capital of the former French colony of Congo enjoyed its quietest day in over a week of ethnic and political bloodletting on Friday and mediators said peace talks would take place in Gabon.

Gunfire rang out sporadically in Brazzaville and the occasional grenade or mortar blast could be heard but residents emerged in parts of the city to inspect the damage and console those who had lost loved ones.

France said in Paris that it would start pulling its troops out of Brazzaville on Sunday. French troops have evacuated 4,300 foreign nationals, including 1,550 French citizens. The government did not say how long the pullout would take.

"The two protagonists and the mediation committee chairman are to meet in Libreville with (Gabon's) President (Omar) Bongo," Hellot Mampouya, a spokesman for Brazzaville mayor and mediation committee chairman Bernard Kolelas, told reporters.
The bloody standoff between supporters of President Pascal Lissouba and his predecessor, former Marxist military leader Denis Sassou Nguesso, dates back to June 5.
The fighting began after the army surrounded Sassou Nguesso's home as part of a crackdown on private militias and unauthorised arms in the runup to a July 27 election.

"The meeting will probably take place on Sunday because tomorrow representatives of Lissouba and Sassou will meet with the mediating committee which will discuss the points which will be on the agenda at the negotiations," Mampouya said.
A Lissouba spokesman said he had heard of the meeting plan but could not confirm Lissouba would attend. Neither Sassou Nguesso nor a spokesman was immediately available for comment.

Supporters of Kolelas, runner-up to Lissouba in a 1992 presidential election, were in the thick of fighting which killed at least 2,000 people after disputed parliamentary elections in 1993. This time they stayed out of the conflict.
Lissouba and Sassou Nguesso told their forces to cease fire on Wednesday.
"The ceasefire (call) seems much better respected than yesterday," Bertin Mulunga, another Kolelas aide, said. "It might be early to be certain but it seems to be taking hold."
Mohamed Sahnoun, the U.N. and Organisation of African Unity special envoy to the region, told Reuters in Kinshasa that he had been in touch with Bongo and all sides in the conflict.
"There's another fire to put out in the region," he said.

Bodies littered city streets. Aid workers and military officials have not been able to reach all areas in order to compile a reliable death toll, which some sources say could run into hundreds and maybe even several thousand.
"Our mission is essentially accomplished but it's possible that there could be some evacuations tomorrow," French army spokesman Henry Pelissier said.
Sassou Nguesso's militia fought in and around the city centre on Thursday. Witnesses and military officials said they had pushed Lissouba's government forces back in places.

Edmond Munungi, another Kolelas aide, said the mediation committee agreed a peace blueprint, envisaging assembly of fighters and mixed patrols. "Both sides have representatives on the committee so we hope this will be respected," he said.
Sassou Nguesso, named president in 1979, bowed to pressure for multi-party politics in 1990 but was among candidates knocked out in the first round of the 1992 poll.
He returned to Congo in January after over a year in France and launched into an undeclared campaign for the presidency.
